beats.say: Hello! Sometimes a frightening email arrives: I hacked your camera, pay or I will publish your private videos.
The email even shows an old password of yours. It usually comes from a data leak years ago.

body.text: I got into your device and recorded private videos with your camera.

beats.say: Emails like this go to thousands of people at once. There is no video from your camera.
The rule: do not pay or reply, change the password, and report work mail to security.

scenes.prompt: Find the scammer's tricks in this email.

body.text: I got into your device and recorded private videos with your camera.
As proof I am writing your password. If you do not want the videos published, send bitcoin worth 1,500 AZN to:
You have 48 hours to pay. Do not show this email to anyone.

spots.label: Old password
spots.explain: This password comes from an old data leak. It does not prove a hack, but change it everywhere you still use it.

spots.label: Camera claim
spots.explain: This is a bluff. The same text goes to thousands of addresses and there is no video.

spots.label: Bitcoin address
spots.explain: A crypto payment cannot be reversed. If you pay, a new demand will follow.

spots.label: 48 hours
spots.explain: The deadline is there to scare you and stop you thinking. Do not pay and do not reply.

scenes.prompt: Match each claim in the email with the truth.

pairs.right: No proof, the text is sent in bulk
Taken from an old data leak

pairs.left: A photo of your house is attached
pairs.right: Address from a leak, photo from a public map
A fake deadline to scare you

scenes.explain: Everything the scammer knows is public or leaked data. It was put together to frighten you.

scenes.title: Your work mail
scenes.intro: You open your work mailbox at the ministry. Choose the right move for each of the four emails.

subject.text: Your password: Gunes2019. You have 48 hours

body.text: I got into your device and recorded private videos with your camera.
If you do not want the videos published, send bitcoin worth 1,500 AZN to: bc1q000000000000000000000000000000demo

actions.label: Report phishing
actions.feedback: Right. The security team can remove the same email from other colleagues' mailboxes too.

actions.label: Reply: show me proof
actions.feedback: A reply shows that your address is active and brings more emails. Do not reply.

actions.label: Delete
actions.feedback: Deleting is fine. In work mail, though, reporting it first is better.

subject.text: Do you see the photo of your house?

body.text: This is your house. I know your address and your password.
Send 1,500 AZN in bitcoin, or the videos will be published.

actions.label: Report phishing
actions.feedback: Right. The house photo comes from a public map, so this is a mass bluff too.

actions.label: Open photo
actions.feedback: The photo is meant to scare you more. Do not open a suspicious attachment, report the email.

actions.label: Reply: I will pay
actions.feedback: Paying or promising to pay brings new demands. Do not pay and do not reply.

body.text: Today some colleagues received extortion emails showing an old password.
Do not pay and do not reply. Send the email with the Report button.
If you still use that password, change it.

actions.label: Mark as safe
actions.feedback: Right. This email asks for nothing, it only repeats the right rules.

actions.label: Report phishing
actions.feedback: Caution is good, but this email comes from your organisation's own address and asks for nothing.

subject.text: Your account is hacked: change your password now

body.text: Received an extortion email? Your account is in danger.
If you do not change it within 30 minutes, the account will be locked.

actions.label: Report phishing
actions.feedback: Well done. This is a second trap that feeds on fear, and the domain is not your organisation's.

actions.label: Open link
actions.feedback: The fake page would have stolen your password. Change it only in the official system you open yourself.

actions.label: Delete
actions.feedback: Deleting is fine. If you report it, other colleagues are protected too.

question.prompt: An extortion email shows a map photo of your house and your address. What does it mean?

options.label: The address came from a leak, the photo from a public map
options.feedback: Right. Knowing your address does not mean your camera was hacked.

options.label: They really are watching, so I have to pay
options.feedback: Paying ends nothing, it brings a new demand. Report the email.

options.label: I should reply and ask who they are
options.feedback: A reply shows your address is active. The scammer will send more emails.

scenes.explain: The scammer combines public and leaked data to create fear. Do not pay or reply, and if you feel in danger, contact the police.

points: A mass email saying I hacked your camera is a bluff: do not pay, do not reply.
If you still use the old password from the email, change it everywhere.
In work mail, report such an email to the security team.
